problem: Existing open-vocabulary ObjectNav methods use RL or map modules with opaque decisions, or use CoT whose structure is implicit and does not separate perception-focused target-environment reasoning from planning-focused environment-action reasoning. Memory designs that compress or textualize history also lose information, which hurts generalization to unseen object categories.
motivation: Agents must decide where to search, why, and which way to go, which depends on two relations: which observed objects and regions relate to the target, and how that understanding turns into actions. Making these relations explicit with structured CoT, plus a memory that keeps target-relevant and current-view-relevant history, should improve success on unseen categories without depth, maps or RL.
key_idea: Train a Qwen2.5-VL-7B model with SFT on a structured CoT dataset (perception, target-environment, environment-action) and a parameter-free similarity-based memory (compress and fuse frames), using only first-person RGB.
insight: Structured CoT is the largest contributor. Without it, val-unseen SR is 14.8 (memory-free model), and with full CoT it reaches 28.4. Adding each CoT component helps monotonically. In the memory ablation, relevance-based fusion of frames beats removal and temporal-interval criteria on SR (44.0 vs 42.0 for temporal removal), while temporal fusion has higher SPL. Compression using both the instruction and the current frame beats instruction-only (42.0 vs 39.8 SR).
method: CoT dataset generation: expert trajectories from HM3D-OVON; a random key frame is the current frame, earlier frames are history, and the next 5 actions are ground truth; Qwen2.5-VL-7B annotates CoT in three parts (environment perception, target-environment relationship, environment-action plan).
CoT curation: entries whose perception section contains hedging words (may, might, indicate, imply) are discarded as hallucinations, leaving about 300K samples.
Frame compression: the previous frame's tokens are reduced to the 30 with the highest average of cosine similarity to the instruction embedding and to the new current frame.

Memory maintenance: when the memory exceeds its limit, the adjacent pair with the highest fusion score is average-pooled into one frame. The score is w1(1-sim to instruction)+w2(1-sim to current)+w3(adjacent similarity), with weights 0.3/0.3/0.4 as in the algorithm. This adds no parameters.

Model and inference: Qwen2.5-VL-7B takes prompt, task, memory frames, current frame and a search instruction, and autoregressively outputs CoT plus discrete actions. Prepending 'Please do not output your thinking process' skips CoT at evaluation for about 2 Hz inference.
Training: 1 epoch of SFT on R2R/RxR plus OVON data, with only the aligner and LLM activated, on 64 H20 GPUs (~1280 GPU hours).

setting.training_data: About 300K CoT-annotated samples from HM3D-OVON expert trajectories (CoT annotated by Qwen2.5-VL-7B), plus R2R/RxR data; SFT only, 1 epoch, simulation only
setting.observation: single first-person monocular RGB (640x520), no depth or odometry

results: Nav-R2 reaches 44.0 SR / 18.0 SPL on OVON val-unseen with RGB only, beating Uni-NaVid (39.5 / 19.8), which is the closest RGB-only baseline, on SR. It also beats depth/map methods Nav-R1 (42.2) and MTU3D (40.8) on val-unseen SR, though those are stronger on val-seen. SPL is comparable or slightly lower.
limitations: SPL is lower than Uni-NaVid and Nav-R1 on val-unseen, and depth/map methods are stronger on val-seen.
Evaluated only on OVON in simulation, with no real-robot tests.
The fast 2 Hz inference mode disables CoT at test time, and the CoT annotations depend on a 7B VLM with heuristic hallucination filtering.
